name: Ray-Centric and Hardware-Accelerated Rendering
text:
# Ray-Centric and Hardware-Accelerated Rendering


## Overview
Ray-centric rendering computes pixel color by tracing rays from the camera through volumetric data and accumulating density and color along the path, typically executed on the GPU for performance. It differs from [splatting](#23-splatting.md) by processing samples per-ray rather than per-primitive, avoiding sorting overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel [G]. It preserves internal volume information, unlike [isosurface extraction](#30-isosurface-extraction.md) methods such as [Marching Cubes](53-marching-cubes.md) [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The family traces rays from the camera through volumetric data to compute pixel color and opacity. Rays are marched through the volume using step-based sampling or [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structures, with contributions accumulated along the ray path. GPU [hardware acceleration](#21075-hardware-acceleration-gpu-opencl.md) is used for parallel execution [S1, unofficial][S2].

## Subtopics

### [Batched Ray Rendering](1547-batched-ray-rendering.md)
[Batched Ray Rendering](#1547-batched-ray-rendering.md) is a memory-management strategy for object-order volume rendering that processes large batches of rays in smaller, fixed-size chunks to prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors on the GPU. It is primarily used during validation and inference phases where full-resolution images must be generated without training-time optimizations like CUDA-accelerated raymarching. It builds on [Ray-Centric and Hardware-Accelerated Rendering](8936-ray-centric-and-hardware-accelerated-rendering.md) by explicitly managing the batch size relative to available VRAM, and differs from [Chunked Trilinear Volume Rendering](2557-chunked-trilinear-volume-rendering.md) by [chunking](#5773-chunking.md) the *rays* (the query set) rather than the *volume data* (the lookup grid). See [Batched Ray Rendering](1547-batched-ray-rendering.md).

### [GPU Implementation Pipeline](2385-gpu-implementation-pipeline.md)
A GPU-accelerated rendering technique that traces rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D volume to compute color and opacity, implemented in a single pass using fragment shaders. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes. It differs from isosurface extraction (e.g., [Marching Cubes](53-marching-cubes.md)) by preserving internal volume information, and from splatting ([Splatting](10-splatting.md)) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than [texture-based splatting](#19892-texture-splatting.md) [G]. See [GPU Implementation Pipeline](2385-gpu-implementation-pipeline.md).

### OptiX Volume Rendering Pipeline
- [S1, unofficial] A volume rendering method implemented using NVIDIA OptiX. It uses a Ray Generation shader, Miss shaders for radiance and shadow, and Hit/Any-Hit/Intersection shaders for volume traversal and shading.
- [S1, unofficial] Initialize shaders: Set `shader_raygen` to `__raygen__default`. Add miss shaders `__miss__radiance` and `__miss__shadow`.
- [S1, unofficial] Configure volume object group: Set `group.type = VOLUME_STRUCTURED_REGULAR`. Assign hit group shaders: Closest Hit `__closesthit__volume_radiance` and `__closesthit__volume_shadow`, Any Hit `__anyhit__volume_radiance` and `__anyhit__volume_shadow`, and Intersection `__intersection__volume`.
- [S1, unofficial] Shader assignments: Ray Gen: `__raygen__default`. Miss: `__miss__radiance`, `__miss__shadow`. Volume Closest Hit: `__closesthit__volume_radiance`, `__closesthit__volume_shadow`. Volume Any Hit: `__anyhit__volume_radiance`, `__anyhit__volume_shadow`. Volume Intersection: `__intersection__volume`.

### Hybrid Splatting/Tracing Rendering
- [S2] A rendering pipeline that rasterizes primary rays for speed and traces secondary rays for lighting effects (reflections/refractions) within the same 3D representation.
- [S2] Compute all primary [ray intersections](#7624-ray-ray-intersection.md) with the scene.
- [S2] Render these primary rays using [rasterization](#15310-rasterization.md) (splatting).
- [S2] Discard Gaussian hits that fall behind a ray's closest intersection.
- [S2] Compute and trace secondary rays using 3DGRT.

## Background
Ray casting and marching are standard techniques for high-quality volume visualization, leveraging the parallel nature of GPU fragment shaders for per-pixel [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) [G]. The specific [GPU implementation pipeline](#2385-gpu-implementation-pipeline.md) utilizes a slab method for AABB intersection and front-to-back [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) within a single fragment shader pass [S2]. The integration of ray tracing APIs like NVIDIA OptiX [S1, unofficial] allows for more complex traversal and shading models, while recent hybrid approaches [S2] combine the speed of rasterization for primary rays with the accuracy of ray tracing for secondary effects like reflections.
